title: The Midnight Shots and the Hostile Witness Box
hook: When thirty-two eyewitnesses recant their testimony and the murder weapon vanishes, appellate courts reconstruct a fatal late-night shooting through unbroken physical evidence.

facts.label: Legal Question
facts.value: Whether an appellate court can convict when primary eyewitnesses turn hostile and the firearm is missing

facts.label: Key Forensic Evidence
facts.value: Ballistic comparison of cartridge cases and matching vehicle window glass shards

summary: In the early morning hours at an exclusive capital restaurant party, a patron demanded alcohol after the bar had closed and supplies were exhausted. When a celebrity bartender politely refused service, the patron drew a small-caliber handgun, fired an initial warning shot into the ceiling, and then discharged a second point-blank shot directly into the victim's temple. The shooter fled into the night after being confronted by restaurant proprietors, and the victim succumbed to brain trauma shortly thereafter.

During the trial, the prosecution suffered an unprecedented evidentiary breakdown when thirty-two witnesses, including direct eyewitnesses who had observed the shooting, recanted their statements and turned hostile in the witness box. A key witness introduced a novel claim that two separate shooters were present, which the defense used to construct a theory that different weapons were fired. Pointing to the hostile testimony and the failure of investigators to recover the firearm, the trial court delivered a comprehensive acquittal of all accused.

On appeal against acquittal, the high court reversed the judgment, and the Supreme Court of India affirmed the conviction. The apex court held that the Latin maxim falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus has no application in Indian courts; judges must separate the grain of truth from the chaff of falsehood in hostile testimony. The bench confirmed that the evidentiary value of a hostile witness's statements is not erased completely, and portions corroborating the prosecution remain fully admissible.

The conviction was firmly anchored in circumstantial and physical evidence that remained untainted by witness intimidation. Forensic experts matched broken glass fragments from the crime scene directly to an abandoned vehicle used by the accused, and ballistics proved that both cartridge cases were fired from a single firearm. The court held that the absence of the murder weapon is not fatal to the prosecution when the presence, motive, and subsequent conduct of the accused are established beyond reasonable doubt.

timeline.title: The Shooting at the Colonnade
timeline.text: A patron discharges two firearm rounds inside an open-air cafe, fatally injuring a bartender after alcohol service is refused.

timeline.title: Recovery of Abandoned Vehicle
timeline.text: Police discover an abandoned vehicle with shattered window glass matching fragments recovered from the restaurant entrance.

timeline.title: Surrender of the Primary Accused
timeline.text: The primary accused surrenders to police authorities following days of abscondence.

timeline.title: Trial Court Acquittal
timeline.text: The trial court acquits all accused, citing hostile eyewitnesses and failure to recover the weapon of offence.

timeline.title: Appellate Reversal by High Court
timeline.text: The high court overturns the acquittal, finding the trial judgment perverse and sentencing the primary accused to life imprisonment.

timeline.title: Supreme Court Affirmation
timeline.text: The Supreme Court of India upholds the conviction, establishing authoritative benchmarks on hostile witnesses and appellate review.

judgment.outcome: The Supreme Court of India dismissed the appeals, upholding the high court's reversal of acquittal and confirming the life sentence for murder.
points: The maxim falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus is not applicable in India, and the credible portions of a hostile witness's testimony may be relied upon.
An appellate court possesses full authority to reverse an acquittal if the trial court's conclusions are perverse, demonstrably unsustainable, or ignore material evidence.
The non-recovery of the weapon of offence is not fatal to the prosecution when ocular presence, motive, ballistics, and conduct are firmly established.
Subsequent conduct, including abscondence and attempting to conceal vehicles, provides strong corroborative evidence of guilt.

principles.name: Rejection of False in One, False in All
principles.latin: falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus
principles.meaning: The doctrine that a witness who lies about one matter is completely untrustworthy does not apply in Indian law; courts must separate truth from falsehood in hostile testimony.
principles.inThisCase: The court relied on the initial admissions and corroborating details provided by witnesses who had otherwise turned hostile to reconstruct the sequence of events.

principles.name: Appellate Power to Reverse Acquittal
principles.meaning: Appellate courts may reappraise evidence and overturn an acquittal when the trial court's reasoning is perverse or ignores vital material facts.
principles.inThisCase: The court affirmed the high court's intervention because the trial court had unreasonably discarded strong circumstantial links and accepted untenable defense theories.

principles.name: Sufficiency of Circumstantial Chain Without Weapon
principles.meaning: Failure to recover the weapon of offence does not weaken the prosecution if the rest of the circumstantial and forensic evidence forms an unbroken chain.
principles.inThisCase: The conviction was sustained despite the missing firearm because ballistics, matching vehicle glass, and immediate post-shooting conduct conclusively established guilt.

takeaways: The testimony of a hostile witness is not wiped off the record and can be relied upon to the extent it supports truth and credible corroboration.
Appellate courts have full jurisdiction to reverse an acquittal when the trial court's judgment is palpably unreasonable or misreads forensic evidence.
A murder conviction can be sustained even if the weapon is never recovered, provided that forensic and circumstantial links remain unbroken.
Perjury proceedings can be initiated against witnesses who deliberately retract sworn police statements during serious criminal trials.

lawNote: The incident took place in April 1999, and the trial and subsequent appeals were governed by the Indian Penal Code, 1860, the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, and the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. The new penal and procedural statutes (Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam) took effect on 1 July 2024 and apply prospectively.
